entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Lasting for a very long time, or happening again and again, so that it seems permanent.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and educated speech: *a perennial problem*, *a perennial favorite*, *a perennial contender*, *perennial complaints*. It can be positive (a dish or a film that is always popular) or tired (a problem nobody ever solves). In gardening, *perennials* are plants that live for more than two years.
entries.pattern: a perennial favorite / problem / contender / question
examples: Macaroni and cheese is a **perennial** favorite on the school lunch menu.
Parking downtown is a **perennial** complaint at every city council meeting.
The team is a **perennial** contender but hasn't won a title in thirty years.

drill.sentence: Whose turn it is to take out the trash is a {{perennial}} argument in our house.
drill.hint: coming back again and again for years (not *recurring*, *constant*, *frequent* or *never-ending*)

entries.related: *recurring* — happening again and again; *chronic* — long-lasting and bad, especially illness; *perpetual* — never ending; *one-off* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Having a lot of experience in a particular activity or job, and therefore skilled and calm in it.
entries.usage: Common in news, job ads and conversation: *a seasoned traveler*, *a seasoned journalist*, *a seasoned pro*, *seasoned investors*. It is positive and almost always goes before the noun. The cooking sense (food *seasoned* with salt and spices) is a separate use.
entries.pattern: a seasoned + traveler / professional / veteran / journalist
examples: As a **seasoned** traveler, she packs everything into one small bag and never checks luggage.
Even **seasoned** hikers can get lost in this canyon when the weather turns.
The hospital hired a **seasoned** nurse to train the new staff in the emergency room.

drill.sentence: The rookie was nervous, but the {{seasoned}} goalie next to him had seen it all before.
drill.hint: with years of practice behind him (not *veteran* or *experienced*)

entries.related: *experienced* — neutral; *veteran* — with long service, also a noun; *battle-hardened* — toughened by difficulties; *green* or *novice* — the opposites.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To officially require something by law, rule or order.
entries.usage: Common in American news, law and policy, often passive or as a compound adjective: *federally mandated*, *state-mandated testing*. After *mandate that*, American English normally uses the base form of the verb: *the law mandates that every school have a nurse*. In conversation, *require* or *make mandatory* sounds more natural.
entries.pattern: mandate something; mandate that + clause; state- / federally mandated
examples: The state **mandates** that all new homes have smoke detectors in every bedroom.
The league now **mandates** helmets for all players under twelve.
Third graders now spend two weeks every spring on **state-mandated** tests.

drill.sentence: A new law will {{mandate}} that all restaurants list calories on their menus.
drill.hint: officially make compulsory (not *require*, *demand* or *order*)

entries.related: *require* — the everyday word; *stipulate* — set a condition, in contracts; *impose* — force a rule or cost on people; *mandatory* — the adjective, required.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make something less extreme or less strong, especially expectations, enthusiasm or criticism, often by balancing it with something else.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports and business writing: *temper expectations*, *temper enthusiasm*, *temper criticism with praise*. The pattern *temper A with B* means balancing A with B, as in *justice tempered with mercy*. In conversation *temper* is mostly a noun (*lose your temper*), so the verb sounds a little formal.
entries.pattern: temper expectations / enthusiasm; temper A with B
examples: The coach tried to **temper** expectations, saying the young team needed a year or two to develop.
She **tempered** her criticism of my essay with a lot of praise for the opening.
Rising mortgage rates have **tempered** enthusiasm among first-time buyers.

drill.sentence: I'd {{temper}} your expectations about the hotel; the photos online were taken twenty years ago.
drill.hint: make less extreme (not *lower*, *manage*, *moderate* or *adjust*)

entries.related: *moderate* — make less extreme, more formal; *tone down* — informal, make less strong; *dampen* — reduce enthusiasm; *heighten* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To keep a feeling, doubt, hope or suspicion in your mind for a long time, often secretly.
entries.usage: Common in writing and educated speech, especially with negative or private feelings: *harbor doubts*, *harbor a grudge*, *harbor resentment*, *harbor ambitions*. It suggests the feeling is kept quietly, not shown openly. In a legal sense, *harbor a fugitive* means hiding a wanted person.
entries.pattern: harbor doubts / a grudge / resentment / suspicions / ambitions
examples: He still **harbors** a grudge against his brother for selling their father's car.
Many fans **harbored** doubts about the new coach, but he won them over by October.
She'd long **harbored** a dream of opening a small bookstore by the sea.

drill.sentence: I never told my parents, but as a kid I {{harbored}} a secret fear that they would split up.
drill.hint: kept quietly in my mind for a long time (not *had*, *held*, *nursed* or *carried*)

entries.related: *nurse* — keep a feeling alive, often a grudge; *cherish* — keep a positive feeling or memory; *entertain* — consider an idea; *let go of* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To add a condition or limit to a statement so that it is less general or less absolute.
entries.usage: Common in academic writing, journalism and careful speech: *qualify a statement*, *let me qualify that*. Speakers use it when they realize they have said too much and want to add an exception. The adjective works the same way: *a qualified yes* or *qualified support* is limited, not complete.
entries.pattern: qualify a statement / claim / remark; a qualified yes / success
examples: I said the food there is the best in town, but let me **qualify** that: the desserts are terrible.
The authors **qualify** their findings by noting that all the patients were over sixty.
Her answer was a **qualified** yes: she'd join the trip if she could get the time off.

drill.sentence: My uncle said he'd never eat sushi, then quickly {{qualified}} the remark: "Well, maybe the cooked kind."
drill.hint: limited it with a condition (not *softened*, *corrected*, *clarified* or *amended*)

entries.related: *hedge* — avoid a firm commitment; *caveat* — a warning or limit added to a statement (noun); *add a proviso* — formal, add a condition; *generalize* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To cause someone or something to be in a particular state or condition, usually a bad one.
entries.usage: Formal and common in news, legal and technical writing, followed by an object and an adjective: *rendered useless*, *rendered obsolete*, *rendered unconscious*, *render someone speechless*. It is stronger and more formal than *make*, and it is often passive. In casual speech it sounds dramatic, so people use it mainly for humor.
entries.pattern: render + object + adjective (useless / obsolete / unconscious / speechless)
examples: Dropping it in the sink **rendered** my new phone completely useless.
Streaming has **rendered** the DVD player almost obsolete.
The blow to the head **rendered** him unconscious for several minutes.

drill.sentence: The snowstorm {{rendered}} the roads impassable, so the wedding guests spent the night at the hotel.
drill.hint: caused to become — formal (not *made* or *left*)

entries.related: *make* — the everyday word; *leave* — often for results (*left him speechless*); *render* also means to provide (*render a service*) or to draw (*a 3D rendering*).

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To deal with questions, calls, complaints or requests as they come, often quickly and skillfully.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and conversation: *field questions*, *field calls*, *field complaints*, *field requests*. It comes from the sports sense of stopping or catching a ball, so it suggests handling many incoming things one after another. It sounds natural in both speech and writing.
entries.pattern: field questions / calls / complaints / requests (from someone)
examples: After her talk, the author spent an hour **fielding** questions from the audience.
My mom has been **fielding** calls from relatives all day about the wedding.
The airline hired extra staff to **field** complaints after the cancellations.

drill.sentence: After the loss, the coach {{fielded}} questions from reporters for twenty minutes and stayed calm the whole time.
drill.hint: caught one after another, like balls in a game (not *answered*, *took*, *handled* or *dealt with*)

entries.related: *handle* — deal with, more general; *take questions* — accept questions, neutral; *deflect* — turn a question away; *dodge* — avoid answering.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To accept and carry a burden, cost or responsibility, often a heavy or unfair one.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation: *shoulder the burden*, *shoulder the cost*, *shoulder the blame*, *shoulder responsibility*. It suggests carrying a heavy load, sometimes for others who are not helping. It is often used to talk about who pays: *taxpayers will shoulder the cost*.
entries.pattern: shoulder the burden / cost / blame / responsibility (for)
examples: After their mother got sick, my older sister **shouldered** most of the caregiving.
Many teachers **shoulder** the cost of classroom supplies themselves, spending hundreds of dollars a year.
The goalkeeper **shouldered** the blame for the loss, though the whole defense played badly.

drill.sentence: When the business failed, he {{shouldered}} the debt himself so his partners wouldn't lose their homes.
drill.hint: put on his own back, like a heavy load (not *carried*, *bore*, *assumed*, *absorbed* or *took on*)

entries.related: *bear* — carry or accept, more formal (*bear the cost*); *take on* — accept a task or responsibility; *shirk* — the opposite, avoid a duty.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To arrange a deal or agreement between other people or groups by talking to both sides.
entries.usage: Common in news about diplomacy, business, labor and sports: *broker a deal*, *broker a ceasefire*, *a deal brokered by* someone. The person doing it is not one of the main parties. The noun *broker* means someone who buys and sells for others, as in *a real estate broker*.
entries.pattern: broker a deal / agreement / ceasefire / truce; brokered by + mediator
examples: My aunt **brokered** a truce between my brothers before Thanksgiving dinner.
The strike ended with a deal **brokered** by a federal mediator.
The bank **brokered** the sale of the family company to a larger competitor.

drill.sentence: The neighbors were about to sue each other until a friend {{brokered}} a compromise over the shared fence.
drill.hint: set up between the two sides (not *negotiated*, *arranged*, *mediated* or *worked out*)

entries.related: *mediate* — help two sides reach agreement; *negotiate* — discuss to reach a deal, often as one side; *facilitate* — make a process easier.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To publicly support, defend and fight for a cause, an idea or a group of people.
entries.usage: Common in news, biographies and speeches: *champion a cause*, *champion the rights of*, *champion reform*, *champion local artists*. It is positive and suggests active, long-term work, not just agreement. A person who does this is *a champion of* the cause.
entries.pattern: champion a cause / the rights of / an idea / someone
examples: She spent her career **championing** the rights of patients with rare diseases.
The local radio station has always **championed** young musicians from the area.
Long before it was popular, he **championed** bike lanes in the city.

drill.sentence: My grandmother {{championed}} recycling in our town long before most people cared about it.
drill.hint: publicly fought for (not *promoted*, *pushed*, *encouraged* or *supported*)

entries.related: *advocate (for)* — speak in support of; *stand up for* — defend, informal; *promote* — help something become known; *oppose* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To try hard to win the support, favor or business of a person or group, for example by paying them attention or offering benefits.
entries.usage: Common in news about politics, business and sports: *court voters*, *court investors*, *court young customers*, *court a free agent*. It suggests a deliberate, sometimes flattering effort. In *court disaster* or *court controversy* it means acting in a way that risks something bad.
entries.pattern: court voters / investors / customers / a player
examples: Car companies are **courting** young buyers with cheap leases and free charging.
Several teams are **courting** the star pitcher, who becomes a free agent in November.
For months, the university **courted** the famous chef to run its new culinary program.

drill.sentence: The new restaurant is {{courting}} families with free kids' meals on weekdays.
drill.hint: trying hard to win over (not *wooing*, *luring*, *targeting* or *attracting*)

entries.related: *woo* — very close, a bit more playful; *cultivate* — build a relationship slowly; *curry favor* — try to please someone in power, critical; *alienate* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To become more important, successful or famous than someone or something, so that they seem less important by comparison.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports and biographies: *eclipse a record*, *be eclipsed by* a rival, *eclipse someone's achievements*. It is often passive and suggests the first thing is overshadowed, not destroyed. In sports, *eclipse a record* simply means beat it.
entries.pattern: eclipse a record / a rival; be eclipsed by
examples: Her younger sister's fame quickly **eclipsed** her own.
He **eclipsed** the old scoring record with three games left in the season.
Online sales have **eclipsed** in-store sales at many big retailers.

drill.sentence: The movie's soundtrack became so popular that it {{eclipsed}} the film itself.
drill.hint: made it seem less important by comparison (not *overshadowed*, *outshone*, *upstaged* or *surpassed*)

entries.related: *overshadow* — very close, also means spoil a happy event (*the news overshadowed the party*); *outshine* — be better than; *surpass* — go beyond a level or record.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To doubt or criticize a decision after it has been made, especially your own or someone else's.
entries.usage: Very common in American conversation, sports and management talk: *second-guess yourself*, *stop second-guessing*, *second-guess the coach*. It suggests unhelpful doubt or criticism with the benefit of hindsight. A second meaning is predicting what someone will do (*try to second-guess the market*).
entries.pattern: second-guess yourself / a decision / someone; stop second-guessing
examples: I picked the apartment quickly, and I've been **second-guessing** myself ever since.
Fans love to **second-guess** the coach's decisions from their couches.
Once you've hired someone, don't **second-guess** every choice they make.

drill.sentence: You studied hard and your first answer was probably right, so don't {{second-guess}} yourself during the exam.
drill.hint: keep doubting your choice after making it (not *doubt* or *question*)

entries.related: *have second thoughts* — begin to doubt a decision; *doubt yourself* — more general; *Monday-morning quarterback* — US, someone who criticizes decisions after the fact.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To avoid dealing with a difficult topic, problem or rule directly, by going around it.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation: *skirt the issue*, *skirt the question*, *skirt the rules*, *skirt the law*. It is critical and suggests evasion. *Skirt around* is also common, especially in speech: *she skirted around the question of money*.
entries.pattern: skirt (around) the issue / question / rules / law
examples: Every time I ask about his ex, he **skirts** the subject and starts talking about work.
The landlord found a way to **skirt** the rent rules by calling the apartment a hotel room.
The CEO **skirted** questions about layoffs during the TV interview.

drill.sentence: At the family reunion, everyone {{skirted}} the topic of my brother's divorce, hoping nobody would bring it up.
drill.hint: went around without addressing (not *avoided*, *dodged* or *sidestepped*)

entries.related: *sidestep* — avoid a question or problem; *dodge* — avoid, informal; *gloss over* — mention briefly to hide details; *address* — the opposite, deal with directly.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To express an idea, feeling or plan clearly and effectively in words.
entries.usage: Common in educated speech and writing: *articulate a vision*, *articulate a concern*, *struggle to articulate* something. It suggests clear expression of something complex, not just speaking. The verb ends in *-layt*, while the adjective (*she's very articulate*) ends in a weak *-lut*.
entries.pattern: articulate a vision / idea / concern / feeling; hard to articulate
examples: She finally **articulated** what had been bothering her about the relationship for months.
The new director **articulated** a clear plan for the museum's next ten years.
Kids often feel things they can't yet **articulate**, so they act out instead.

drill.sentence: He knew the plan was wrong, but he couldn't quite {{articulate}} why until the next morning.
drill.hint: find the clear words for (not *explain*, *express*, *say* or *put into words*)

entries.related: *express* — more general; *put into words* — plain, informal; *verbalize* — say aloud, often feelings; *convey* — communicate a meaning or feeling.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To treat an idea, possibility or piece of information as unimportant, untrue or unlikely, and so not consider it seriously.
entries.usage: Common in news, analysis and serious conversation: *discount the possibility*, *discount a theory*, *discount someone's opinion*. It is very often negative: *we can't discount the risk*, *I wouldn't discount him*. Its stress can fall on either syllable, and it sounds natural in both writing and speech.
entries.pattern: discount the possibility / a theory / someone's views; can't / wouldn't discount
examples: Police haven't **discounted** the possibility that the fire was set on purpose.
Don't **discount** the underdogs; they've beaten better teams this year.
She felt her boss **discounted** her ideas just because she was the youngest person in the room.

drill.sentence: The forecast looks clear, but I wouldn't {{discount}} the chance of a storm in the mountains this time of year.
drill.hint: treat as unimportant or unlikely (not *rule out*, *dismiss* or *ignore*)

entries.related: *dismiss* — reject as not worth considering; *rule out* — exclude completely; *disregard* — pay no attention to; *take into account* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: New, original and different from anything known or done before.
entries.usage: Common in science, business and journalism: *a novel approach*, *a novel idea*, *a novel virus*, *novel solutions*. It usually goes before the noun and is mostly positive, though it can simply mean *unfamiliar*. In casual speech it sounds a little formal or playful, as in *Well, that's a novel excuse*.
entries.pattern: a novel approach / idea / method / solution
examples: Paying kids to read is a **novel** idea, but will it make them love books?
The team used a **novel** approach: training the model on synthetic data first.
"My dog ate my phone" — well, that's a **novel** excuse.

drill.sentence: The chef has a {{novel}} way of cooking eggs: she poaches them in olive oil instead of water.
drill.hint: never seen before (not *new*, *unique*, *unusual*, *original* or *creative*)

entries.related: *innovative* — introducing new ideas, also about people; *original* — not copied; *groundbreaking* — new and important; *conventional* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Similar enough to something that it makes you think of it.
entries.usage: Common in reviews, travel writing and educated speech: *reminiscent of the 1980s*, *a taste reminiscent of*, *eerily reminiscent of*. It almost always takes *of*, and it describes the thing that causes the memory, not the person remembering. Typical adverbs are *strongly*, *vaguely* and *eerily*.
entries.pattern: be reminiscent of + noun; strongly / vaguely / eerily reminiscent of
examples: This soup is **reminiscent of** the one my grandmother used to make.
Her voice is **reminiscent of** a young Joni Mitchell.
The market panic was eerily **reminiscent of** 2008.

drill.sentence: With its steep hills and cable cars, the old neighborhood is strongly {{reminiscent of}} San Francisco.
drill.hint: making you think of something similar (not *evocative of*)

mistake.wrong: I'm reminiscent of my childhood when I smell fresh bread.
mistake.right: The smell of fresh bread is reminiscent of my childhood.
mistake.why: The thing that triggers the memory is *reminiscent of* something; a person who remembers *reminisces about* it.

entries.related: *evocative of* — bringing a feeling or image to mind, literary; *redolent of* — formal, smelling of or suggesting; *reminisce* — the verb, talk about the past.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Using too much force, control or pressure, so that it is clumsy or unfair.
entries.usage: Common in news and everyday criticism of authorities, managers and parents: *heavy-handed tactics*, *a heavy-handed response*, *heavy-handed regulation*. It suggests poor judgment as well as force. In reviews it describes a message or symbol that is far too obvious: *the ending is a bit heavy-handed*.
entries.pattern: a heavy-handed approach / response / tactics / message
examples: Suspending twenty kids for one water-balloon fight seemed a bit **heavy-handed** to most parents.
The movie's message about greed is so **heavy-handed** that it feels like a lecture.
Security at the stadium was **heavy-handed**, with guards shouting at fans just for standing up.

drill.sentence: Instead of a {{heavy-handed}} lecture, my dad just asked me what I thought had gone wrong.
drill.hint: clumsy and too forceful (not *stern*, *harsh* or *long*)

entries.related: *high-handed* — arrogant, ignoring others' views; *ham-fisted* — clumsy, informal; *draconian* — extremely harsh, about laws; *a light touch* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Acting or speaking mainly to benefit yourself, often while pretending to help others or to be objective.
entries.usage: Common in news, analysis and conversation as a criticism: *a self-serving argument*, *a self-serving account*, *self-serving motives*. It often describes explanations and statements, not just people: *his version of events is a bit self-serving*. In psychology, *self-serving bias* means taking credit for success and blaming others for failure.
entries.pattern: a self-serving argument / account / decision / motive
examples: The CEO's memoir is entertaining but **self-serving**; every mistake is someone else's fault.
Calling the fee increase "good for customers" sounds pretty **self-serving** to me.
My cousin's advice to sell the family house seemed **self-serving**, since he wanted to buy it.

drill.sentence: The company's study claiming that its own energy drink improves focus is obviously {{self-serving}}.
drill.hint: mainly benefiting itself (not *biased*)

entries.related: *selfish* — caring only about yourself, more personal; *biased* — unfairly favoring one side; *self-interested* — more neutral; *selfless* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Covering all cases or all people in a group, with no exceptions.
entries.usage: Common in news, law and policy: *a blanket ban*, *a blanket policy*, *a blanket statement*, *blanket immunity*. It always comes before the noun. It is often critical, suggesting that a rule is too broad and ignores important differences.
entries.pattern: a blanket ban / policy / rule / statement
examples: The park has a **blanket** ban on dogs, even small ones on a leash.
Saying that all teenagers are lazy is a **blanket** statement that just isn't true.
The airline's **blanket** refund policy covers every cancellation, whatever the reason.

drill.sentence: The school's {{blanket}} rule against phones means students can't even text their parents after practice.
drill.hint: covering everyone, with no exceptions (not *total*, *strict* or *general*)

entries.related: *across-the-board* — affecting everyone equally; *sweeping* — wide-ranging; *wholesale* — complete, often too extensive; *case-by-case* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Depending on something else happening or being true first.
entries.usage: Formal, common in contracts, business and official writing: *the offer is contingent on a background check*, *contingent upon approval*. *On* and *upon* are both standard; *upon* is more formal. In American real estate, *contingent* alone means an offer has been accepted but still depends on conditions such as an inspection.
entries.pattern: be contingent on / upon + noun or -ing
examples: The job offer is **contingent on** passing a background check.
Our trip to Japan is **contingent on** my new passport arriving in time.
The team's playoff hopes are **contingent on** two other teams losing this weekend.

drill.sentence: His parents said their help with tuition was {{contingent on}} his keeping his grades above a B.
drill.hint: depending on — formal (not *conditional on*, *dependent on* or *tied to*)

entries.related: *conditional on* — very close; *dependent on* — more general; *subject to* — legal, can be changed by (*subject to approval*); *unconditional* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Similar to something, or of the same kind, often in an important way.
entries.usage: Formal, common in essays, journalism and educated speech for making a comparison: *akin to theft*, *something akin to panic*. It comes after *be* or after a noun, never before a noun, and it almost always takes *to*. *Something akin to* is a common way to describe a feeling you can't name exactly.
entries.pattern: be akin to + noun / -ing; something akin to + feeling
examples: For my dad, asking for directions is **akin to** admitting defeat.
When the band walked on stage, the crowd made a noise **akin to** a jet taking off.
Charging customers for tap water feels **akin to** theft.

drill.sentence: When the lights went out in the crowded subway, she felt something {{akin to}} panic rising in her chest.
drill.hint: of the same kind as — formal (not *like*, *close to*, *approaching* or *similar to*)

entries.related: *similar to* — neutral; *comparable to* — able to be compared, often in size or quality; *tantamount to* — formal, equal in effect, usually bad; *unlike* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The way someone weighs the different factors, risks and benefits before making a decision.
entries.usage: Common in political, business and sports journalism: *the political calculus*, *the calculus changes*, *shift someone's calculus*. It suggests a cool, strategic process rather than emotion. It sounds analytical, so in conversation people more often say *the math* (*the math doesn't work*).
entries.pattern: the (political / economic) calculus; change / shift the calculus (for someone)
examples: Once the baby arrived, the **calculus** of living in the city changed completely.
Higher gas prices have shifted the **calculus** for many commuters, who now take the train.
The coach's **calculus** was simple: go for it on fourth down, because a field goal wouldn't win the game.

drill.sentence: With flights this cheap, the {{calculus}} of driving versus flying to Grandma's has changed.
drill.hint: the weighing of costs and benefits (not *math*, *economics* or *equation*)

entries.related: *trade-off* — a balance between two things; *cost-benefit analysis* — a formal comparison of costs and gains; *the math* — informal, the numbers behind a decision.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An idea or category that people have created, rather than something that exists naturally or objectively.
entries.usage: Common in academic writing, especially sociology and psychology, and in educated debate: *a social construct*, *a cultural construct*, *a theoretical construct*. The noun is stressed on the first syllable, the verb *to construct* on the second. Saying something *is a construct* can sound dismissive, as in the online joke *time is a construct*.
entries.pattern: a social / cultural / theoretical construct
examples: The weekend is a social **construct**; for farmers, Saturday is just another workday.
In psychology, "intelligence" is a **construct** that researchers measure in different ways.
"I'm late, but time is a **construct** anyway," my roommate joked as we ran for the bus.

drill.sentence: The idea of a "guilty pleasure" is a cultural {{construct}}: there's nothing wrong with loving cheesy pop songs.
drill.hint: a made-up category (not *invention*, *creation* or *concept*)

mistake.why: As with many two-syllable noun–verb pairs (*a record, to record*), the noun is stressed on the first syllable.

entries.related: *concept* — a general idea; *convention* — an accepted custom; *fiction* — something invented, more critical.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The belief that you deserve special treatment or privileges without having earned them.
entries.usage: Very common in American conversation and journalism as a criticism: *a sense of entitlement*, *pure entitlement*, *the entitlement is unreal*. The adjective *entitled* (*he's so entitled*) is even more frequent in speech. In US politics, *entitlements* also means government benefit programs, which is a separate meaning.
entries.pattern: a sense of entitlement; sheer / pure entitlement; be / act entitled
examples: He expected a promotion after six months with no extra effort; the **entitlement** was unbelievable.
Cutting the line and then demanding a discount — that's pure **entitlement**.
Some parents worry that giving kids everything they want creates a sense of **entitlement**.

drill.sentence: The guest who angrily demanded a refund because the free breakfast had no lobster showed an incredible sense of {{entitlement}}.
drill.hint: believing you deserve special treatment (not *privilege* or *self-importance*)

entries.related: *privilege* — real advantages, not just an attitude; *arrogance* — believing you are better than others; *self-importance* — an exaggerated sense of your own value; *humility* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A fact or situation that clearly shows that a system, group or person has failed or is seriously wrong.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, opinion writing and serious speech: *an indictment of* + a system, *a damning indictment*, *a sad indictment of*. The subject is usually a fact or a statistic, not a person. The *c* is silent; the legal meaning is a formal charge of a serious crime.
entries.pattern: an indictment of + system / society / priorities; a damning / sad indictment
examples: The fact that teachers buy their own classroom supplies is an **indictment** of how we fund schools.
Two-hour waits in the emergency room are a damning **indictment** of the hospital's management.
When the kids' favorite restaurant is the gas station, that's a sad **indictment** of my cooking.

drill.sentence: That a city this rich has no public swimming pool is a sad {{indictment}} of its priorities.
drill.hint: a clear sign that something is badly wrong (not *reflection* or *comment*)

mistake.why: The *c* is silent and the *i* sounds as in *write*, just as in the verb *indict*.

entries.related: *testament to* — proof of something good; *reflection on* — something that shows a quality, good or bad; *condemnation* — strong criticism.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: In reality or in practice, even if not officially or by name.
entries.usage: Very common in news, business and conversation: *it's effectively a ban*, *he's effectively the boss*, *the decision effectively ends the project*. It usually comes just before the verb or the noun phrase it describes. Be careful: it also means *successfully* (*she handled it effectively*), so place it where the meaning is clear.
entries.pattern: effectively + noun phrase / verb (it's effectively a ban; effectively ended)
examples: The fee is so high that it's **effectively** a ban on street vendors downtown.
His wife does all the planning and hiring, so she's **effectively** running the business.
Missing the penalty **effectively** ended their chances of making the playoffs.

drill.sentence: The road closure {{effectively}} cuts the village off from the hospital for three months.
drill.hint: in practice, if not officially (not *basically*, *essentially*, *practically* or *virtually*)

entries.related: *in effect* — same meaning, a bit more formal; *virtually* — almost completely; *de facto* — formal, existing in fact but not by law; *officially* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To cause continual trouble, pain or worry to someone or something over a long period.
entries.usage: Very common in news and sports, often passive: *plagued by injuries*, *plagued by delays*, *plagued with problems*. It suggests repeated, annoying trouble rather than one disaster. With a person as subject, it means to bother someone again and again: *reporters plagued her with questions*.
entries.pattern: be plagued by / with + problems / injuries / doubts; something plagues someone
examples: The new subway line has been **plagued** by delays and cost overruns.
He was a brilliant player whose career was **plagued** by knee injuries.
Doubts about whether she'd made the right choice **plagued** her for weeks.

drill.sentence: Our vacation was {{plagued}} by bad luck: lost luggage, a canceled ferry and three days of rain.
drill.hint: one problem after another (not *marred*, *dogged*, *beset*, *hit* or *ruined*)

entries.related: *beset* — formal, surrounded by problems; *dog* — follow and trouble (*dogged by scandal*); *haunt* — worry someone for a long time; *bedevil* — cause a lot of trouble.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Enormous in effect or importance, causing a change that shakes the existing situation.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and business: *a seismic shift*, *seismic change*, *a seismic impact*. It is strong and a bit dramatic, used mainly for changes in markets, culture, sports and technology. The literal sense is about earthquakes (*seismic activity*).
entries.pattern: a seismic shift / change / event / impact (in something)
examples: Streaming has brought **seismic** changes to the movie business, and many theaters have closed.
The trade of their best player marked a **seismic** shift in the league's balance of power.
Remote work has had a **seismic** impact on downtown restaurants.

drill.sentence: The new highway caused a {{seismic}} shift in the town's economy, as shoppers drove past to the big malls.
drill.hint: earthquake-like in its effect (not *huge*, *major*, *dramatic*, *significant* or *tectonic*)

entries.related: *tectonic* — slow but huge, also from geology; *sea change* — a complete transformation; *momentous* — very important; *incremental* — the opposite, in small steps.

entries.label: adjective and noun
entries.meaning: A very large number of things: *myriad* + plural noun means *countless* or *very many*.
entries.usage: Formal and common in writing: *myriad reasons*, *myriad ways*, or as a noun, *a myriad of options*. Some style guides prefer *myriad reasons* to *a myriad of reasons*, but both are standard and have a long history. In conversation, *tons of* or *all kinds of* sounds more natural.
entries.pattern: myriad + plural noun; a myriad of + plural noun
examples: There are **myriad** reasons to move to a smaller city, from cheaper rent to shorter commutes.
On a clear night in the desert, you can see **myriad** stars.
The new phone offers a **myriad** of settings that most people will never touch.

drill.sentence: The festival offers {{myriad}} ways to spend a weekend: concerts, food trucks, craft workshops and more.
drill.hint: too many to count — formal (not *countless*, *numerous*, *endless* or *many*)

entries.related: *countless* — too many to count; *numerous* — many, formal; *a host of* — a large number of; *a handful of* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A pause or break in an activity, especially a long one, after which the activity is expected to continue.
entries.usage: Common in entertainment news and conversation: *the band went on hiatus*, *a two-year hiatus*, *after a long hiatus*. It suggests that the activity will probably return. It sounds slightly formal or journalistic; in casual speech people also say *a break* or *time off*.
entries.pattern: on hiatus; go on / take a hiatus; after a (long) hiatus
examples: The band went on **hiatus** in 2019 and just announced a reunion tour.
After a five-year **hiatus**, she's started painting again.
The show is on **hiatus** until the fall while the actors film other projects.

drill.sentence: The podcast has been on {{hiatus}} since the host had twins, but fans hope it'll be back next year.
drill.hint: stopped for now, but expected to return (not *break*, *pause* or *hold*)

entries.related: *break* — the everyday word; *sabbatical* — paid leave for study or travel; *lull* — a quiet period in an activity; *suspension* — an official stop.

entries.label: preposition / adverb
entries.meaning: Despite something; it can come before the noun or, very often, after it (*the rain notwithstanding*).
entries.usage: Formal, used mainly in legal documents, journalism and academic writing: *notwithstanding the delays*, *these concerns notwithstanding*. Placing it after the noun is common and sounds elegant. In conversation it sounds stiff or comic, so people say *despite* or *even so*.
entries.pattern: notwithstanding + noun; noun + notwithstanding
examples: The rain **notwithstanding**, the parade went ahead and thousands of people showed up.
**Notwithstanding** the rumors, the coach says he isn't going anywhere.
The contract states that, **notwithstanding** any other clause, either side may cancel with thirty days' notice.

drill.sentence: Her nerves {{notwithstanding}}, she gave a beautiful speech at her sister's wedding.
drill.hint: despite — formal, placed after the noun (not *aside*)

entries.related: *despite* / *in spite of* — the everyday words; *nonetheless* — however, at the start or end of a sentence; *regardless of* — without being affected by.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To pay careful attention to advice or a warning and act on it.
entries.usage: Formal and a little literary, common in news and serious writing: *heed a warning*, *heed advice*, *heed the call*. It is very frequent in the negative, especially in reports of accidents and disasters: *failed to heed warnings*. As a noun it appears in *pay heed to* and *take heed*.
entries.pattern: heed a warning / advice / the call; fail to heed; pay heed to
examples: Doctors warned him to slow down, but he didn't **heed** their advice until his first heart attack.
The team finally **heeded** its fans' complaints and brought back the old uniforms.
Hundreds of volunteers **heeded** the call to help clean up the beach after the oil spill.

drill.sentence: Thousands of residents refused to {{heed}} the evacuation order and stayed in their homes as the hurricane approached.
drill.hint: act on a warning — formal (not *obey*, *follow*, *respect* or *listen to*)

mistake.wrong: She didn't heed to the warning.
mistake.why: The verb *heed* takes a direct object; *to* belongs only in the noun phrase *pay heed to*.

entries.related: *mind* — pay attention to, informal (*mind the step*); *take into account* — consider; *disregard* or *ignore* — the opposites.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Always, in every case, without exception; often used when the result is predictable.
entries.usage: Common in writing and educated speech, often with mild humor or resignation: *it invariably rains when we plan a picnic*. It usually goes before the main verb or after *be*. It is stronger than *usually*, but people often use it a little loosely to mean *almost always*.
entries.pattern: invariably + verb; be invariably + adjective / noun
examples: Whenever I wash my car, it **invariably** rains the next day.
My grandfather's stories **invariably** end with a lesson about saving money.
Meetings that start late **invariably** run late too.

drill.sentence: At the grocery store, I {{invariably}} pick the slowest line, no matter how carefully I choose.
drill.hint: in every single case (not *always*, *inevitably* or *somehow*)

entries.related: *inevitably* — as was certain to happen, about one result; *consistently* — in the same way over time; *without fail* — informal, every time; *occasionally* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very strict, precise and demanding; used about rules, standards, tests and controls.
entries.usage: Formal, common in law, regulation, science and business: *stringent requirements*, *stringent standards*, *stringent safety checks*. It describes rules and conditions, not people; for a person, say *strict*. It often appears in comparatives: *more stringent rules*.
entries.pattern: stringent rules / standards / requirements / tests / checks
examples: Baby car seats have to pass **stringent** crash tests before they can be sold.
The co-op board has **stringent** requirements: buyers need two years of mortgage payments in the bank.
Since the outbreak, imported food has faced more **stringent** checks at the border.

drill.sentence: Organic farms must meet {{stringent}} standards on pesticides to keep their certification.
drill.hint: very demanding and exact (not *strict*, *rigorous*, *tough* or *high*)

mistake.wrong: Our math teacher is very stringent.
mistake.right: Our math teacher is very strict.
mistake.why: *Stringent* describes rules, standards and tests; for people, natives say *strict*.

entries.related: *strict* — the everyday word, also for people; *rigorous* — thorough and careful; *exacting* — demanding great care; *lax* — the opposite, not strict enough.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Courage and determination that make you keep going when things are hard, often for a long time.
entries.usage: Very common in American sports, business and education talk: *show grit*, *take grit*, *grit and determination*. Since psychologist Angela Duckworth's research on *grit* (passion and perseverance for long-term goals), it has also been a buzzword in American schools. The phrase *grit your teeth* means to accept something unpleasant with determination.
entries.pattern: show / have grit; it takes grit to …; grit and determination
examples: Finishing nursing school while working nights took real **grit**.
My grandmother raised six kids alone; she had more **grit** than anyone I know.
The underdogs didn't have much talent, but they showed incredible **grit** in the second half.

drill.sentence: Learning to walk again after the accident took months of pain and pure {{grit}}.
drill.hint: stubborn courage to keep going (not *determination*, *willpower*, *persistence* or *guts*)

entries.related: *perseverance* — formal, continuing despite difficulty; *resilience* — recovering after problems; *guts* — informal, courage; *tenacity* — refusing to give up.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To gather courage, energy, support or strength with effort, often with difficulty.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing: *muster (up) the courage to*, *muster the energy*, *muster support*, *all the … I could muster*. It suggests the amount is limited and hard to find. It comes from gathering soldiers for inspection, which also gives *pass muster*, meaning to be good enough.
entries.pattern: muster (up) the courage / energy / strength to; muster support; all the X I could muster
examples: It took me a week to **muster** the courage to ask her out.
With all the enthusiasm she could **muster**, she said, "What a lovely sweater, Grandma."
The proposal couldn't **muster** enough support to pass the city council.

drill.sentence: After the night shift, he could barely {{muster}} the energy to make dinner.
drill.hint: bring out from limited reserves (not *find*, *summon* or *gather*)

entries.related: *summon* — formal, call up courage or strength; *work up* — gradually develop (*work up the nerve*); *pass muster* — be acceptable; *rally* — gather support.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Based on wrong ideas or poor judgment, often although the intention was good.
entries.usage: Common in news, opinion writing and polite criticism: *a misguided attempt*, *misguided policies*, *well-meaning but misguided*. It is softer than *stupid* or *wrong*, because it suggests good intentions. It usually describes plans, beliefs and efforts rather than people.
entries.pattern: a misguided attempt / belief / effort; well-meaning but misguided
examples: In a **misguided** attempt to help, my dad reorganized my whole kitchen while I was at work.
The ban on swings at the playground was well-meaning but **misguided**.
Many people hold the **misguided** belief that you can't get sunburned on a cloudy day.

drill.sentence: Feeding bread to ducks is kind but {{misguided}}; it's actually bad for them.
drill.hint: based on poor judgment (not *mistaken*, *wrong* or *unwise*)

entries.related: *mistaken* — wrong about a fact; *ill-advised* — unwise, formal; *misplaced* — given to the wrong thing (*misplaced loyalty*); *sound* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Dealing with real, important or meaningful matters, rather than details, form or appearances.
entries.usage: Formal, common in politics, law, business and academic discussion: *substantive changes*, *a substantive discussion*, *substantive issues*, *substantive feedback*. It is often contrasted with *cosmetic* or *procedural*. Do not confuse it with *substantial*, which means large in size or amount.
entries.pattern: substantive changes / issues / discussion / feedback
examples: The new owners promised **substantive** changes, but so far they've only repainted the lobby.
Most of the comments on my novel draft were about typos; only one reader gave **substantive** feedback.
We dated for two years before we had a **substantive** conversation about money.

drill.sentence: The meeting with the landlord was friendly, but nothing {{substantive}} came out of it; the heater is still broken.
drill.hint: of real importance (not *concrete*, *meaningful*, *useful*, *significant* or *real*)

mistake.why: *Substantial* means large; *substantive* means dealing with important content.

entries.related: *substantial* — large in size or amount; *meaningful* — important, less formal; *cosmetic* — affecting only the surface; *superficial* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Sensible and careful, especially in avoiding risks and planning for the future.
entries.usage: Common in finance, law, medicine and official advice: *it would be prudent to …*, *a prudent decision*, *prudent with money*. It sounds formal and a little cautious, so in casual speech people say *smart* or *a good idea*. The noun is *prudence*.
entries.pattern: it's / it would be prudent to + verb; a prudent move / decision; prudent with money
examples: With prices rising, it might be **prudent** to lock in a fixed-rate mortgage now.
She's always been **prudent** with money, so she was ready when she lost her job.
Packing an extra battery for the camping trip was a **prudent** move; my phone died on day one.

drill.sentence: Before a long road trip, it's {{prudent}} to check the tire pressure and the spare.
drill.hint: careful about future risk (not *wise*, *smart*, *sensible* or *advisable*)

entries.related: *sensible* — reasonable, everyday; *cautious* — avoiding risk; *judicious* — showing good judgment, formal; *reckless* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A government policy of strong cuts in public spending, usually to reduce debt.
entries.usage: Common in economic and political news, especially about Europe after 2008: *austerity measures*, *years of austerity*, *an austerity budget*. It is a loaded word: supporters call the same policy *fiscal responsibility*, while opponents blame it for hardship. It is also used jokingly for a household that is spending less.
entries.pattern: austerity measures / budget / program; years of austerity; impose austerity
examples: Under the city's new **austerity** budget, two libraries will close and weekend bus service will be cut.
Greece went through years of **austerity** after its first bailout in 2010.
After the wedding and the new car, we're in a period of household **austerity**: no takeout, no vacations.

drill.sentence: To pay off its debts, the government cut pensions and public salaries in a tough {{austerity}} program that lasted five years.
drill.hint: severe spending cuts (not *cost-cutting* or *savings*)

entries.related: *cutbacks* — reductions in spending; *belt-tightening* — informal, spending less; *fiscal restraint* — a more positive term; *stimulus* — the opposite, spending to boost the economy.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Exploiting people who are weaker, poorer or less informed in order to gain money or power.
entries.usage: Common in news, law and consumer advice: *predatory lending*, *predatory pricing*, *predatory journals*, *predatory behavior*. It is strongly negative and suggests deliberate targeting of vulnerable people. In business, *predatory pricing* means selling very cheaply to destroy competitors.
entries.pattern: predatory lending / lenders / pricing / journals / behavior
examples: **Predatory** lenders target people with bad credit, offering quick loans at 400 percent interest.
A **predatory** contractor talked my elderly neighbor into a twenty-thousand-dollar roof repair she didn't need.
**Predatory** journals charge researchers to publish but skip real peer review.

drill.sentence: The city passed a law to stop {{predatory}} towing companies from charging drivers hundreds of dollars to get their cars back.
drill.hint: exploiting people who can't fight back (not *shady*, *greedy*, *rogue* or *unscrupulous*)

entries.related: *exploitative* — unfairly using people; *unscrupulous* — without moral principles; *predator* — the noun; *ethical* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Intended to punish, often more harshly than seems fair or necessary.
entries.usage: Formal, common in law, politics and business news: *punitive measures*, *punitive tariffs*, *punitive damages*. In American law, *punitive damages* are money a court orders as punishment, beyond paying for the harm. In everyday contexts it criticizes a rule or fee that feels like a punishment.
entries.pattern: punitive measures / damages / fines / fees
examples: The jury awarded the family ten million dollars in **punitive** damages.
A thirty-five-dollar overdraft fee feels **punitive** for a student who's two dollars short.
Taking away his phone for a month seemed a bit **punitive** for one late night.

drill.sentence: The library dropped its {{punitive}} late fees after realizing they kept poorer families from borrowing books.
drill.hint: meant to punish (not *harsh*, *steep* or *excessive*)

entries.related: *punishing* — physically exhausting (*a punishing schedule*); *harsh* — severe; *corrective* — meant to fix rather than punish; *lenient* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Extremely slow, especially in a frustrating way.
entries.usage: Common in journalism and witty conversation, very often in *at a glacial pace*, *glacial progress* and *glacial speed*. It is a humorous exaggeration that compares something to the slow movement of a glacier. It can also describe a cold, unfriendly manner (*a glacial stare*), which is a separate use.
entries.pattern: at a glacial pace / speed; glacial progress
examples: Service at the DMV was **glacial**: three hours to renew a driver's license.
Progress on the new bridge has been **glacial**: ten years of planning and no construction yet.
In some fields, peer review is **glacial**; a year from submission to decision is normal.

drill.sentence: The renovation is moving at a {{glacial}} pace; the kitchen has been torn apart since March.
drill.hint: like ice moving down a mountain (not *snail's* or *slow*)

entries.related: *at a snail's pace* — informal, very slow; *sluggish* — slow and lacking energy; *painstaking* — slow because careful; *breakneck* — the opposite (*at breakneck speed*).

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The meanings of words and phrases; in everyday arguments, a disagreement only about which word to use, not about the real issue.
entries.usage: In everyday speech it is mostly dismissive: *that's just semantics*, *let's not argue about semantics*, meaning the difference in wording does not matter. Be careful, because this can sound rude if the word choice really matters to the other person. In linguistics and computer science, *semantics* is the study of meaning.
entries.pattern: that's (just) semantics; argue about / over semantics
examples: Whether you call it a "fee" or a "surcharge," I'm still paying it; the rest is **semantics**.
We spent twenty minutes arguing about whether a hot dog is a sandwich, which is really just **semantics**.
In linguistics, **semantics** studies meaning, while syntax studies sentence structure.

drill.sentence: "I didn't lie; I just didn't tell you." "That's {{semantics}}, and you know it."
drill.hint: a difference in words, not in facts (not *splitting hairs*, *a technicality* or *nonsense*)

entries.related: *splitting hairs* — arguing about tiny differences; *wordplay* — clever use of words; *pedantic* — too concerned with small details or rules; *substance* — the real content.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Including many different styles, ideas or sources, chosen from a wide range.
entries.usage: Common and usually positive in conversation and lifestyle writing: *eclectic taste in music*, *an eclectic mix*, *an eclectic collection*, *eclectic decor*. It suggests interesting variety and personal choice rather than a random mess. Typical partners are *mix*, *taste*, *collection* and *style*.
entries.pattern: an eclectic mix / collection / style; eclectic taste (in something)
examples: Her playlist is pretty **eclectic**: jazz, K-pop, country and a bit of opera.
The restaurant serves an **eclectic** menu, from Korean tacos to Nigerian stews.
Their apartment has an **eclectic** style, with antique chairs next to modern art.

drill.sentence: The neighborhood flea market sells an {{eclectic}} mix of vintage clothes, old records and handmade jewelry.
drill.hint: varied, drawn from many sources (not *interesting*, *odd* or *unusual*)

entries.related: *diverse* — varied, often about people; *wide-ranging* — covering many topics; *motley* — varied in a messy way, often negative; *uniform* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Not clear or transparent, so that it is hard to understand how something works or why decisions are made.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, business and tech writing about systems and institutions: *an opaque process*, *opaque pricing*, *opaque rules*. It is critical and suggests a lack of openness or accountability. The literal meaning, not letting light through (*opaque glass*), is common too, and the noun is *opacity*.
entries.pattern: an opaque process / system / pricing / decision
examples: Hospital pricing is so **opaque** that patients rarely know the cost until the bill arrives.
The airline's rules for upgrades are completely **opaque**; nobody knows who gets one.
Deep learning models can be **opaque**, even to the people who built them.

drill.sentence: The school's admissions process is so {{opaque}} that parents have no idea why one child gets in and another doesn't.
drill.hint: impossible to see into (not *unclear*, *murky*, *mysterious* or *secretive*)

entries.related: *murky* — unclear and possibly dishonest; *obscure* — not well known or hard to understand; *impenetrable* — impossible to understand; *transparent* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Regularly found in, and typical of, a particular place, group or situation; usually describes a problem that is hard to remove.
entries.usage: Formal, common in news, medicine and biology: *corruption is endemic*, *endemic poverty*, *endemic in the region*. It suggests that a problem is built into a place or system, not temporary. In medicine an *endemic* disease is always present in an area, unlike an *epidemic*, a sudden outbreak; in biology, *endemic to* means found only there.
entries.pattern: be endemic in / to + place or group; endemic corruption / poverty / disease
examples: Malaria is still **endemic** in parts of sub-Saharan Africa.
Burnout seems **endemic** in the restaurant industry, where twelve-hour shifts are normal.
The kiwi is **endemic** to New Zealand; it lives nowhere else in the wild.

drill.sentence: Cheating was so {{endemic}} in the local cycling club that new riders assumed everyone did it.
drill.hint: built into the group, always present (not *widespread*, *common*, *rampant* or *rife*)

entries.related: *rife* — full of something bad; *rampant* — spreading out of control; *epidemic* — a sudden, widespread outbreak; *native to* — the neutral biology term.
